Palindrome Number.statement: Return whether an integer reads the same from left to right and right to left.
Palindrome Number.idea: Instead of reversing the whole number (which could overflow 32-bit integers), reverse only the back half of the digits and compare it with the front half.
steps: If x < 0 or (x % 10 == 0 and x != 0), it cannot be a palindrome, so return false.
While x > revertedNumber, pop the last digit of x and append it to revertedNumber.
When the loop finishes, check if x == revertedNumber (even length) or x == revertedNumber / 10 (odd length).
Palindrome Number.python:
# Approach 2: Reverse half of the digits
def is_palindrome(x: int) -> bool:
    # Negative numbers and multiples of 10 (except 0) are not palindromes
    if x < 0 or (x % 10 == 0 and x != 0):
        return False

    reverted = 0
    while x > reverted:
        reverted = reverted * 10 + (x % 10)
        x //= 10

    # Even number of digits: x == reverted
    # Odd number of digits: x == reverted // 10
    return x == reverted or x == reverted // 10

Reverse Integer.statement: Reverse the decimal digits of a signed 32-bit integer; return zero if the result is outside the signed 32-bit range.
Reverse Integer.idea: Repeatedly peel off the last digit with % 10 and push it onto the reversed number with * 10, checking for 32-bit overflow before actually performing the multiplication.
steps: While x is not 0, extract the last digit: pop = x % 10.
Check if ans * 10 + pop will overflow 32-bit signed integer boundaries.
Update ans = ans * 10 + pop and x = x / 10.
Reverse Integer.python:
# Approach 2: Arithmetic pop and push with boundary guard
def reverse(x: int) -> int:
    sign = -1 if x < 0 else 1
    x = abs(x)
    ans = 0

    while x != 0:
        pop = x % 10
        x //= 10
        ans = ans * 10 + pop

    ans *= sign
    # 32-bit signed range check
    if ans < -2**31 or ans > 2**31 - 1:
        return 0
    return ans

Count Negative Numbers in an Array.statement: Count how many values in an array are strictly less than zero.
Count Negative Numbers in an Array.idea: Start from the bottom-left (or top-right) corner. Since rows and columns are sorted, if grid[r][c] is negative, all elements below it in that column are also negative! We can count them all in O(1) and move left.
steps: Start at the bottom-left corner: r = m - 1, c = 0.
If grid[r][c] < 0, then every element in this row from c onwards is negative (since row is descending). Add (cols - c) to count and move up: r--.
Else, the number is non-negative, so we must move right: c++.
Repeat until r < 0 or c >= cols.
Count Negative Numbers in an Array.python:
# Approach 3: Staircase walk from bottom-left
def count_negatives(grid):
    rows = len(grid)
    cols = len(grid[0])
    r = rows - 1
    c = 0
    count = 0

    while r >= 0 and c < cols:
        if grid[r][c] < 0:
            # Everything to the right in this row is also negative
            count += (cols - c)
            r -= 1  # Move up to row above
        else:
            c += 1  # Need more negative, move right
    return count

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Nested Loops
approaches.idea: Iterate through every single row and every column in the 2D matrix, checking each cell to see if it is negative.
pros: Works even if the matrix is unsorted
cons: Completely ignores the sorted property of the matrix
Slow O(m * n) time
steps: Loop through each row i from 0 to m - 1.
Loop through each column j from 0 to n - 1.
approaches.timeExplanation: Visits every single cell in the m x n grid.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Only a single counter variable is maintained.

approaches.idea: Since each row is sorted in descending order, we can binary search for the first negative number in each row. All numbers to its right will also be negative.
pros: Significantly faster than brute force when rows are long
cons: Still doesn't utilize the column-sorted property
O(m log n) time
steps: For each row, use binary search to locate the index of the first negative number.
If first negative is at index k, then (n - k) elements in this row are negative.
Add this to the total count.
approaches.timeExplanation: Binary search of length n is performed across m rows.
approaches.spaceExplanation: No extra space allocated.

approaches.name: Approach 3: Staircase Walk (Most Optimal)
approaches.idea: Start from the bottom-left (or top-right) corner. Since rows and columns are sorted, if grid[r][c] is negative, all elements below it in that column are also negative! We can count them all in O(1) and move left.
pros: Takes full advantage of both row and column sorting
cons: Requires understanding 2D matrix staircase navigation
steps: Start at the bottom-left corner: r = m - 1, c = 0.
If grid[r][c] < 0, then every element in this row from c onwards is negative (since row is descending). Add (cols - c) to count and move up: r--.
Else, the number is non-negative, so we must move right: c++.
Repeat until r < 0 or c >= cols.
approaches.timeExplanation: In each step we either move up one row or right one column, taking at most m + n steps.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Only pointers r and c are used.

Binary Search.statement: Find the index of target in an ascending sorted array of distinct integers, or return -1 if absent.
Binary Search.idea: Maintain two boundary pointers, low and high. Repeatedly probe the midpoint and shrink the search window by half until target is found or bounds cross.
steps: If nums[mid] < target, search right half: low = mid + 1.
Else search left half: high = mid - 1.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Linear Search (Brute Force)
approaches.idea: Scan through the array from left to right, comparing each element with the target until a match is found.
pros: Works even if the array is unsorted
cons: Fails to utilize the sorted property
Slow O(N) time for large arrays
steps: Iterate through the array with index i from 0 to N - 1.
If nums[i] == target, return index i immediately.
If the loop ends without finding target, return -1.
approaches.timeExplanation: In the worst case, we inspect all N elements.
approaches.spaceExplanation: No additional data structures are used.

approaches.name: Approach 2: Recursive Binary Search (Better)
approaches.idea: Halve the search space in each step using recursion. Compare target with the middle element, then recurse on either the left or right subarray.
cons: Uses O(log N) stack frames for recursive function calls
steps: If low > high, target is not present, return -1.
If target < nums[mid], recurse on left: helper(low, mid - 1).
Else recurse on right: helper(mid + 1, high).
approaches.timeExplanation: The search interval is cut in half at each recursive depth.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Recursion call stack takes depth proportional to log N.

Merge Sort.statement: Return an ascending sorted copy of an integer array using divide and conquer.
Merge Sort.idea: Allocate a single auxiliary buffer once at the start of the sort. Reuse this buffer across all merge steps to eliminate repeated dynamic allocations.
steps: Allocate helper buffer of size N.
In merge(low, mid, high), copy elements to helper buffer.
Use two pointers to place elements back in sorted order into original array.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Out-of-Place Divide & Conquer (Standard)
approaches.idea: Recursively split the array in half, sort each half independently, and merge them back together by creating new temporary subarrays at each level.
pros: Classic guaranteed O(N log N) sorting algorithm
Stable sort (preserves relative order of equal elements)
cons: Allocates new subarrays at every recursive step, increasing memory overhead
steps: If the array has 1 or 0 elements, it is already sorted; return.
Create left and right copies, and recursively sort both.
Merge the two sorted halves back into the original array.
approaches.timeExplanation: The array is divided into log N levels, and each level merges N total elements.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Temporary arrays store elements during merges.
approaches.python:
# Approach 1: Merge sort with slicing
def merge_sort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr
    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])

    # Merge sorted pieces
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result

approaches.name: Approach 2: In-Place Buffer Merge Sort (Optimal Memory)
approaches.idea: Allocate a single auxiliary buffer once at the start of the sort. Reuse this buffer across all merge steps to eliminate repeated dynamic allocations.
pros: Avoids continuous heap allocations during recursion
Faster in practice due to better cache locality
Maintains stable O(N log N) performance
cons: Requires passing indices and buffer pointer through recursive calls
steps: Allocate helper buffer of size N.
In merge(low, mid, high), copy elements to helper buffer.
Use two pointers to place elements back in sorted order into original array.
approaches.timeExplanation: Log N division levels with linear merge at each step.
approaches.spaceExplanation: One single reusable buffer of size N is shared by all recursive frames.

Power of Two.statement: Return whether n is a positive integer equal to two raised to a nonnegative integer power.
Power of Two.idea: In binary, a power of two has exactly one set bit (e.g. 8 is 1000). Subtracting 1 flips that bit and sets all lower bits (7 is 0111). Therefore, n & (n - 1) will always equal 0!
steps: Return true if both conditions hold, false otherwise.
Power of Two.python:
# Approach 2: Bit trick n & (n - 1) (Optimal)
def is_power_of_two(n: int) -> bool:
    # Check positive and only one bit set
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0

pros: Intuitive and directly follows the mathematical definition of powers of two
Works naturally across all programming languages
cons: Requires a while loop running up to 31 iterations
Slower than bit manipulation

After the loop, return true if n == 1, else false.
approaches.timeExplanation: We divide n by 2 in each iteration, running at most 31 times for a 32-bit integer.
approaches.spaceExplanation: No additional memory allocated.

approaches.name: Approach 2: Bit Manipulation n & (n - 1) (Optimal)
approaches.idea: In binary, a power of two has exactly one set bit (e.g. 8 is 1000). Subtracting 1 flips that bit and sets all lower bits (7 is 0111). Therefore, n & (n - 1) will always equal 0!
pros: Runs in O(1) single CPU instruction
cons: Must remember to check n > 0 first to filter negative numbers and 0
steps: Return true if both conditions hold, false otherwise.

Remove Duplicates.statement: Remove repeated values from a sorted array in place. Return k such that its first k elements contain the distinct values in order.
Remove Duplicates.idea: Since the array is already sorted, duplicate numbers are adjacent! Keep a slow pointer for the position of the last unique element, and a fast pointer scanning forward.
steps: If nums[fast] != nums[slow], increment slow and set nums[slow] = nums[fast].
Return slow + 1 (the count of unique elements).

approaches.name: Brute force: build a temporary unique array
approaches.idea: Scan the sorted input from left to right. Append a value to a temporary array only when it differs from the last kept value, then copy that unique prefix back into nums.
pros: Easy to reason about because the input and result stay separate during the scan
Preserves the original order of the distinct values
cons: Uses O(N) extra space for the temporary result
Reads the values once to build the result and again to copy it back
steps: Start with an empty Unique[] array and a read pointer at the first input value.
Compare each input value with the last value in Unique[]; append it only when it is new.
Copy the unique values back into the first k positions of nums, one write at a time.
Return k, the number of distinct values; values after index k - 1 are ignored.

Reverse String.statement: Reverse an array of characters in place.
Reverse String.idea: Place one pointer left at index 0 and another pointer right at index n - 1. Swap s[left] and s[right], then advance left and retreat right until they meet in the middle.

# Approach 2: Two pointers swap in-place (Optimal)
def reverse_string(s):
    left = 0
    right = len(s) - 1

    while left < right:
        s[left], s[right] = s[right], s[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1

approaches.name: Approach 2: Two Pointers In-Place Swap (Optimal)

# Approach 2: Two pointers swap in-place (Optimal)
def reverse_string(s):
    left = 0
    right = len(s) - 1

    while left < right:
        s[left], s[right] = s[right], s[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1

Merge Sorted Arrays.statement: Merge nums2 into nums1 in ascending order. nums1 starts with m sorted values and has n reserved slots at the end.
Merge Sorted Arrays.idea: Both inputs are already sorted. The three approaches differ in whether they ignore that order, use a safe temporary result, or use nums1’s free tail to merge in place.
steps: Place i at the last initialized value in nums1, j at the last value in nums2, and w at the last nums1 slot.
Write the larger value into nums1[w].
Move only the source pointer that supplied the value, then move w left.
Stop when j < 0; any remaining nums1 prefix is already in the correct place.
Merge Sorted Arrays.python:
# Optimal: choose the largest remaining value and fill from the back.
def merge(nums1, m, nums2, n):
    i = m - 1  # Last initialized nums1 value.
    j = n - 1  # Last nums2 value.
    w = m + n - 1  # Rightmost output slot.
    while j >= 0:
        if i >= 0 and nums1[i] > nums2[j]:
            nums1[w] = nums1[i]
            i -= 1
        else:
            nums1[w] = nums2[j]
            j -= 1
        w -= 1
    return nums1

approaches.name: Approach 1: Append and Sort (Brute Force)
approaches.idea: Use nums1's reserved tail to append nums2, then ask the standard library to sort all values. This is the easiest baseline, but it throws away the fact that both input ranges are already sorted.
pros: Short and easy to reason about
Provides a useful baseline before using the sorted-input property
cons: Re-sorts values that were already sorted
The sort implementation may allocate temporary memory
steps: Copy nums2 into nums1 beginning at index m, one value per step.
approaches.timeExplanation: Copying is O(n), then sorting all m + n elements costs O((m + n) log(m + n)); the sort dominates.
approaches.spaceExplanation: The sort implementation may use stack or temporary memory. Exact auxiliary space depends on the language runtime and its sorting algorithm.

approaches.name: Approach 2: Forward Merge with a Temporary Array (Better)
approaches.idea: Use the sorted order directly: compare the smallest unmerged values, append the smaller one to a new array, then copy that completed result back into nums1. The extra buffer avoids overwriting either source.
pros: Runs in linear time by using the sorted input ranges
Makes the merge order straightforward to visualize
cons: Allocates a second array of m + n values
Copies the merged values back into nums1
steps: Start i and j at the beginnings of nums1 and nums2.
Compare nums1[i] and nums2[j]; append the smaller value to Merged[].
Append the remaining tail after one source is exhausted.
Copy Merged[] back into nums1 one slot at a time.
approaches.timeExplanation: Each source value is read once, each output value is appended once, then the result is copied back once.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Merged[] stores all m + n output values while the two inputs remain available.

approaches.name: Approach 3: Three Pointers from the Back (Optimal)
approaches.idea: The largest remaining value must go into the rightmost open slot. Compare the tails and write from right to left, using nums1's padding so no unread value is overwritten.
pros: Linear time with one placement per value
Uses the existing padding; no extra result array is needed
cons: The pointer invariant takes care to understand
The loop must continue until nums2 is exhausted
steps: Place i at the last initialized value in nums1, j at the last value in nums2, and w at the last nums1 slot.
Write the larger value into nums1[w].
Move only the source pointer that supplied the value, then move w left.
Stop when j < 0; any remaining nums1 prefix is already in the correct place.
approaches.timeExplanation: Every value is considered and written at most once; the loop ends as soon as nums2 is exhausted.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Only i, j, and w are added. The reserved cells already inside nums1 are the output buffer.

# Optimal: choose the largest remaining value and fill from the back.
def merge(nums1, m, nums2, n):
    i = m - 1  # Last initialized nums1 value.
    j = n - 1  # Last nums2 value.
    w = m + n - 1  # Rightmost output slot.
    while j >= 0:
        if i >= 0 and nums1[i] > nums2[j]:
            nums1[w] = nums1[i]
            i -= 1
        else:
            nums1[w] = nums2[j]
            j -= 1
        w -= 1
    return nums1

# Approach 3: Fast & Slow pointers (Optimal)
def middle_node(head):
    slow = head
    fast = head

    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next       # Advance 1 node
        fast = fast.next.next  # Advance 2 nodes

    return slow

# Approach 1: Store in list

    while head:

        head = head.next

    curr = head
    while curr:

        curr = curr.next
    curr = head

    return curr

# Approach 3: Iterative 3 pointers (Optimal)
def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head

    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next  # Save next node

        prev = curr      # Move prev forward

approaches.python:
# Approach 1: Reverse using a stack
def reverse_list(head):
    if not head:
        return None
    stack = []
    while head:
        stack.append(head)
        head = head.next
    new_head = stack.pop()
    curr = new_head
    while stack:
        curr.next = stack.pop()
        curr = curr.next
    curr.next = None
    return new_head

    new_head = reverse_list(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head

Palindrome Linked List.statement: Return whether the node values in a singly linked list form a palindrome.
Palindrome Linked List.idea: Find the middle of the list using slow/fast pointers. Reverse the second half of the list in place, then compare the first half and the reversed second half node by node.

Compare nodes from head and reversed second half.

Palindrome Linked List.python:
# Approach 2: Reverse second half in place (Optimal)
def is_palindrome(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return True

    slow = fast = head
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next

    prev = None
    curr = slow.next
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt

    p1, p2 = head, prev
    while p2:
        if p1.val != p2.val:
            return False
        p1 = p1.next
        p2 = p2.next

    return True

Rotate List.statement: Rotate a singly linked list right by k positions, with k nonnegative.
Rotate List.idea: Count length N and find the tail. Connect tail.next = head to form a circular ring. The new head will be at index (N - k % N). Walk to the new tail at index (N - k % N - 1), break the ring, and return the new head.

Compute effective rotation steps: k = k % N. If k == 0, return head.

# Approach 2: Ring and Break (Optimal)
# Close the list into a circle, then cut at the new tail
def rotate_right(head, k):
    if not head or not head.next or k == 0:
        return head

    # 1. Measure length and find tail
    n = 1
    tail = head
    while tail.next:
        tail = tail.next
        n += 1

    # 2. Modulo rotation count
    k = k % n
    if k == 0:
        return head

    # 3. Form circular loop
    tail.next = head

    # 4. Move to new tail position
    steps = n - k
    new_tail = tail
    for _ in range(steps):
        new_tail = new_tail.next

    # 5. Break circular loop
    new_head = new_tail.next
    new_tail.next = None
    return new_head

# Approach 2: Built-in Search (Optimal)

def find_words_containing(words, x):
    return [i for i, word in enumerate(words) if x in word]

Split a String in Balanced Strings.statement: Given a balanced string made of L and R, split it into the maximum number of nonempty substrings, each with equal numbers of L and R.
Split a String in Balanced Strings.idea: Treat 'R' as +1 and 'L' as -1. Whenever the running balance returns to 0, we have discovered the shortest possible balanced substring, so we increment our answer.
steps: Iterate through each character: add 1 if 'R', subtract 1 if 'L'.
Whenever balance == 0, we completed a balanced segment: count++.
Split a String in Balanced Strings.python:
# Approach 1: Running Balance Counter (Optimal)
# Track balance between 'R' and 'L'
def balanced_string_split(s: str) -> int:
    balance = 0
    count = 0

    for ch in s:
        balance += 1 if ch == 'R' else -1
        # Balanced group completed
        if balance == 0:
            count += 1

    return count

Swap characters at left and right while left < right.

Sum of Beauty of All Substrings.statement: For every nonempty substring of a lowercase string, define beauty as its largest character frequency minus its smallest positive character frequency. Return the sum of all beauties.
Sum of Beauty of All Substrings.idea: For every starting index i, expand the substring to the right with index j. Update the character frequency count incrementally. In each step, the beauty is (max frequency - min non-zero frequency).

Initialize frequency array of size 26 to 0.
For each end index j from i to N - 1:
Calculate maxFreq and minFreq among present characters.
Sum of Beauty of All Substrings.python:
# Approach 1: Incremental Frequency Scanning (Optimal)
# Count frequencies incrementally for each start position
def beauty_sum(s: str) -> int:
    total_beauty = 0
    n = len(s)

    for i in range(n):
        count = [0] * 26
        for j in range(i, n):
            count[ord(s[j]) - ord('a')] += 1
            freqs = [c for c in count if c > 0]
            total_beauty += max(freqs) - min(freqs)

    return total_beauty

# Approach 2: Separate Substring Extraction (Brute Force)
# Generate each substring and count with Counter
from collections import Counter

def beauty_sum_brute(s: str) -> int:
    total = 0
    n = len(s)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n + 1):
            sub = s[i:j]
            counts = Counter(sub).values()
            total += max(counts) - min(counts)
    return total

Decode String.statement: Decode a valid encoded string where k[part] means part repeated k times. Bracketed expressions can nest, and repeat counts can have multiple digits.
Decode String.idea: Use two stacks: one for repeating counts (countStack) and one for intermediate strings (stringStack). When encountering '[', push the current string and count; when encountering ']', pop and repeat the substring.
steps: If digit, build multi-digit number k = k * 10 + digit.
If '[', push k to countStack and currStr to stringStack; reset k = 0, currStr = ''.
If ']', pop prevStr and repeatCount; currStr = prevStr + currStr repeated repeatCount times.
Decode String.python:
# Approach 1: Two Stacks (Optimal)
# Maintain stack of numbers and stack of previous strings
def decode_string(s: str) -> str:
    count_stack = []
    string_stack = []
    curr_str = ""
    k = 0

    for ch in s:
        if ch.isdigit():
            k = k * 10 + int(ch)
        elif ch == '[':
            count_stack.append(k)
            string_stack.append(curr_str)
            curr_str = ""
            k = 0
        elif ch == ']':
            count = count_stack.pop()
            prev_str = string_stack.pop()
            curr_str = prev_str + curr_str * count
        else:
            curr_str += ch

    return curr_str

Reorganize String.statement: Rearrange a lowercase string so no adjacent characters are equal. Return any valid arrangement, or an empty string if impossible.
Reorganize String.idea: Greedily place the most frequent remaining character. Use a max-heap of character frequencies. In each step, pop the most frequent character, place it, and hold it until the next step so it cannot be placed adjacent to itself.

# Approach 1: Max Heap (Optimal)
# Greedily place the most frequent available character
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def reorganize_string(s: str) -> str:
    counts = Counter(s)
    max_freq = max(counts.values())
    if max_freq > (len(s) + 1) // 2:
        return ""

    heap = [(-freq, ch) for ch, freq in counts.items()]
    heapq.heapify(heap)

    res = []
    prev_cnt, prev_ch = 0, ""

    while heap:
        neg_cnt, ch = heapq.heappop(heap)
        res.append(ch)

        if prev_cnt < 0:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (prev_cnt, prev_ch))

        prev_cnt = neg_cnt + 1
        prev_ch = ch

    return "".join(res)

# Approach 1: Minimum Bound Repetition (Optimal)
# Repeat 'a' to match length of 'b', checking at most count and count + 1
import math

def repeated_string_match(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    count = math.ceil(len(b) / len(a))
    curr = a * count

    if b in curr:
        return count
    if b in (curr + a):
        return count + 1

    return -1

# Approach 2: Monotonic Stack (Optimal)
# Monotonic stack of day indices
def daily_temperatures(temperatures):
    n = len(temperatures)
    ans = [0] * n
    stack = []  # Stores indices

    for i, temp in enumerate(temperatures):
        while stack and temp > temperatures[stack[-1]]:
            prev = stack.pop()
            ans[prev] = i - prev
        stack.append(i)

    return ans

approaches.idea: Repeatedly scan the entire grid. On each round, mark any fresh orange adjacent to a rotten orange as newly rotten (e.g. state 3). After the scan, change all 3s to 2s. Stop when no new oranges rot.

Much slower than BFS

Square Root of X.statement: For nonnegative integer x, return the floor of its square root.
Square Root of X.idea: Search in the range [1, x]. In each step, test mid = left + (right - left) / 2. If mid * mid <= x, record mid as potential answer and search right; else search left.
steps: If mid <= x / mid: ans = mid, left = mid + 1.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Linear Scan (Brute Force)
approaches.idea: Test integers i = 1, 2, 3... until i * i > x. The previous integer (i - 1) is the integer square root.
pros: Extremely simple to code and trace
cons: O(sqrt(X)) runtime is slow for large 32-bit values like x = 2^31 - 1
steps: If i > x / i, return i - 1.
approaches.timeExplanation: Loops up to sqrt(X) iterations.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Only a single loop counter.

approaches.name: Approach 2: Binary Search (Optimal)
approaches.idea: Search in the range [1, x]. In each step, test mid = left + (right - left) / 2. If mid * mid <= x, record mid as potential answer and search right; else search left.
pros: O(log X) runtime (at most 31 iterations for 32-bit integers)
cons: Must guard against integer multiplication overflow with long long or division
steps: If mid <= x / mid: ans = mid, left = mid + 1.
approaches.timeExplanation: Halves the search space in each iteration.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Uses only three integer pointer variables.

Guess Higher or Lower.statement: Find a hidden number in 1 through n using guess(mid): -1 means mid is too high, +1 too low, and 0 correct.
Guess Higher or Lower.idea: Binary search between 1 and n. In each step, guess mid. If guess returns -1, our pick was too high (right = mid - 1); if 1, too low (left = mid + 1); if 0, we found it!

approaches.name: Approach 1: Linear Guessing (Brute Force)
approaches.idea: Guess every number starting from 1 up to n sequentially until the API returns 0.
pros: Simple and requires no state tracking
Guaranteed to eventually hit the target
cons: O(N) time complexity is far too slow when n is up to 2^31 - 1
steps: For num = 1 to n: call guess(num). If guess(num) == 0, return num.

approaches.spaceExplanation: No extra storage.

approaches.name: Approach 2: Binary Search (Optimal)
approaches.idea: Binary search between 1 and n. In each step, guess mid. If guess returns -1, our pick was too high (right = mid - 1); if 1, too low (left = mid + 1); if 0, we found it!
pros: O(log N) runtime (at most 32 API calls)
cons: Must avoid overflow when calculating mid

Search in Rotated Sorted Array.statement: Find target in a rotated ascending array of distinct integers, returning its index or -1.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array.idea: In any rotated sorted array, splitting at mid always leaves at least ONE half completely sorted! Identify the sorted half and check if target falls inside it; if so, search it; otherwise, search the other half.
steps: If nums[low] <= target < nums[mid], high = mid - 1; else low = mid + 1.
If nums[mid] < target <= nums[high], low = mid + 1; else high = mid - 1.

First Bad Version.statement: Versions 1 through n are good until one version becomes bad, after which all are bad. Use is_bad(version) to find the first bad version.
First Bad Version.idea: Since all versions after a bad version are also bad, the problem has monotonic boolean structure [false, false, ..., true, true]. Binary search finds the boundary in O(log N) calls.
steps: Set left = 1, right = n, ans = n.
If isBadVersion(mid): ans = mid, right = mid - 1.

Find Peak Element.statement: Return any index whose value is strictly larger than its neighbors. Adjacent values differ and out-of-range neighbors count as negative infinity.
Find Peak Element.idea: Compare mid with mid + 1. If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], we are on an upward slope, so a peak MUST exist to the right (left = mid + 1). If nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1], we are on a downward slope, so a peak exists at mid or to the left (right = mid).

approaches.name: Approach 1: Linear Scan (Brute Force)
approaches.idea: Traverse the array and return the first element that is strictly greater than its right neighbor: nums[i] > nums[i + 1]. The first such index is guaranteed to be a peak.
cons: O(N) runtime scans the entire array in worst case

If loop finishes, the last element nums[N-1] is the peak.
approaches.timeExplanation: Single pass through array.

approaches.name: Approach 2: Binary Search on Slope (Optimal)
approaches.idea: Compare mid with mid + 1. If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], we are on an upward slope, so a peak MUST exist to the right (left = mid + 1). If nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1], we are on a downward slope, so a peak exists at mid or to the left (right = mid).
pros: Works even though array is unsorted

Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array.statement: Return the smallest value in a nonempty rotated ascending array of distinct integers.
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array.idea: Compare nums[mid] with nums[right]. If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum MUST lie strictly in the right half (left = mid + 1). If nums[mid] <= nums[right], the minimum is at mid or in the left half (right = mid).

cons: O(N) runtime fails to take advantage of the rotated sorted structure

approaches.name: Approach 2: Binary Search against Right Boundary (Optimal)
approaches.idea: Compare nums[mid] with nums[right]. If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum MUST lie strictly in the right half (left = mid + 1). If nums[mid] <= nums[right], the minimum is at mid or in the left half (right = mid).
pros: Clean logic without tracking special cases

Find Peak in a Mountain Array.statement: Return the summit index in an array that strictly increases and then strictly decreases.
Find Peak in a Mountain Array.idea: In a mountain array, if arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1], we are on the uphill climb, so peak is to the right (left = mid + 1). If arr[mid] > arr[mid + 1], we are on the downhill slope, so peak is at mid or to the left (right = mid).

Single Element in a Sorted Array.statement: In a sorted array, every value appears exactly twice except one. Return that singleton.
Single Element in a Sorted Array.idea: Before the single element, pairs always start at even indices (0, 2, 4...) and end at odd indices (1, 3, 5...). After the single element, this pattern shifts! We test if mid's partner is at the expected index (mid ^ 1). If they match, the single element is to the right.

approaches.name: Approach 1: XOR / Linear Scan (Brute Force / Bitwise)
approaches.idea: XOR all elements in the array. Since identical pairs cancel to 0 (x ^ x = 0), the single element will be the final result. Alternatively, step in increments of 2 to check pairs.
pros: Simple and works even if array were unsorted
cons: O(N) runtime ignores the sorted property of the input
steps: For each num in nums: ans ^= num.
approaches.timeExplanation: XORs all N elements.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Stores single integer XOR accumulator.

# Approach 1: Bitwise XOR
# XOR cancellation across the array
def single_non_duplicate_xor(nums):
    ans = 0
    for x in nums:
        ans ^= x
    return ans

Find k Closest Elements.idea: The answer is a contiguous subarray of size k. Use binary search to find the optimal starting index 'left' in the range [0, N - k]. Compare x - arr[mid] with arr[mid + k] - x to decide which direction shifts closer to x.
steps: If x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x: left = mid + 1.

approaches.idea: Sort the array based on absolute difference |num - x|. Take the first k elements, and sort them in ascending order.

Sort sliced k elements ascending and return.

Takes full advantage of the already sorted input array

Two Sum.statement: Return the zero-based indices of two distinct array elements whose sum equals target. The standard problem guarantees one answer.
Two Sum.idea: For each number x at index i, its required complement is target - x. Check if complement already exists in our hash map; if yes, return both indices! Otherwise, record map[x] = i.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Check All Pairs (Brute Force)
approaches.idea: Use two nested loops to check every possible pair of elements (i, j). If nums[i] + nums[j] == target, return [i, j].
pros: Simple and exhaustive: guaranteed to find the solution
cons: O(N²) quadratic time complexity causes TLE on large arrays

If nums[i] + nums[j] == target, return [i, j].
Return empty list if no pair found.
approaches.timeExplanation: Evaluates N*(N - 1)/2 pairs.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Zero extra space allocated.

approaches.name: Approach 2: Two Pointers with Sorting (Better)
approaches.idea: Store numbers with their original indices and sort them. Place one pointer at the start and one at the end, moving inwards based on sum.
pros: Shows the two-pointer technique on sorted data
O(N log N) is faster than brute force
cons: Requires extra array to preserve original indices
Slower than hash map
steps: Pair each number with its original index and sort.
If sum < target left++; else right--.
approaches.timeExplanation: Sorting pairs takes O(N log N).
approaches.spaceExplanation: Stores copy of elements with indices.

approaches.name: Approach 3: One-Pass Hash Map (Most Optimal)
approaches.idea: For each number x at index i, its required complement is target - x. Check if complement already exists in our hash map; if yes, return both indices! Otherwise, record map[x] = i.
pros: Optimal O(N) time in a single pass
The gold standard for Two Sum
cons: Requires hash table lookups
approaches.timeExplanation: Single pass through array with O(1) average map operations.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Stores at most N elements in hash map.

Two Sum II.statement: In an ascending sorted array, return the one-based indices of two distinct elements whose sum equals target.
Two Sum II.idea: Place one pointer at start (left = 0) and one at end (right = N - 1). If sum == target, return indices. If sum < target, increment left to increase sum; if sum > target, decrement right to decrease sum.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Binary Search for Complement (Better)
approaches.idea: For each element numbers[i], use binary search to look for (target - numbers[i]) in the subarray to the right (i + 1 .. N - 1).
pros: O(N log N) time, much faster than O(N²) nested loops
cons: Slower than two pointers O(N)
steps: For each i from 0 to N - 2: complement = target - numbers[i].
Binary search complement in range [i + 1, N - 1].
If found at index j, return [i + 1, j + 1] (1-based).
approaches.timeExplanation: N elements each taking O(log N) binary search.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Stores only loop pointers.

approaches.name: Approach 2: Two Pointers from Ends (Optimal)
approaches.idea: Place one pointer at start (left = 0) and one at end (right = N - 1). If sum == target, return indices. If sum < target, increment left to increase sum; if sum > target, decrement right to decrease sum.
pros: Guaranteed to find the unique pair
cons: Requires sorted array

Is Subsequence.idea: Use two pointers i (for s) and j (for t). Advance j on every step; whenever s[i] == t[j], advance i. If i reaches s.length, all characters of s appeared in t in order.

approaches.idea: Use two pointers i (for s) and j (for t). Advance j on every step; whenever s[i] == t[j], advance i. If i reaches s.length, all characters of s appeared in t in order.

approaches.idea: Preprocess t into a hash map where each character maps to a sorted list of its indices. For each character in s, binary search (upper_bound) for the smallest index strictly greater than the previous matched index.
pros: Extremely fast for multiple incoming queries s1, s2... against a fixed large t

For each c in s: binary search in map[c] for index > currIdx; if none, return false; update currIdx.

approaches.python:
# Approach 2: Binary Search over Index Map
# Binary search using bisect for follow-up queries
from collections import defaultdict
import bisect

def is_subsequence_map(s: str, t: str) -> bool:
    pos = defaultdict(list)
    for i, c in enumerate(t):
        pos[c].append(i)

    prev = -1
    for c in s:
        if c not in pos:
            return False
        lst = pos[c]
        idx = bisect.bisect_right(lst, prev)
        if idx == len(lst):
            return False
        prev = lst[idx]

    return True

Find Index of First Occurrence in String.idea: Slide a window of size M (length of needle) across haystack. At each index i from 0 to N - M, check if the substring matches needle.

If haystack[i .. i + M - 1] == needle, return i.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Sliding Window Substring Match (Optimal / Standard)
approaches.idea: Slide a window of size M (length of needle) across haystack. At each index i from 0 to N - M, check if the substring matches needle.
pros: Runs in O(N * M) worst case but O(N) average case with early mismatch exit
cons: Worst-case quadratic comparisons on pathological repetitive inputs (e.g. 'aaaa...a' and 'aaaab')

If haystack[i .. i + M - 1] == needle, return i.

approaches.idea: Build the Longest Prefix Suffix (LPS) array for needle. When a mismatch occurs after j matches, use lps[j - 1] to avoid re-checking characters that have already been matched.

cons: Requires precomputing the LPS table

On match, i++, j++. If j == needle.length, return i - j.
On mismatch: if j > 0, j = lps[j - 1]; else i++.

Intersection of Two Linked Lists.statement: Return the first node shared by two acyclic singly linked lists, comparing node identity rather than values.
Intersection of Two Linked Lists.example: A and B share the same tail node 8 → return that node
Intersection of Two Linked Lists.idea: Two pointers pA and pB start at headA and headB. When pA reaches the end of list A, redirect it to headB. When pB reaches the end of list B, redirect it to headA. Both pointers travel exactly len(A) + len(B) steps, so they align and meet at the intersection node!

# Approach 2: Two Pointers Path Equalization (Optimal)
# Equalize distances travelled: a + c + b = b + c + a
def get_intersection_node(headA, headB):
    pA, pB = headA, headB

    while pA != pB:
        pA = pA.next if pA else headB
        pB = pB.next if pB else headA

    return pA

Traverse list B: if current node pointer is in hash set, return it.
If end of B reached without match, return null.

# Approach 1: Hash Set of Visited Nodes
# Set lookup on node references
def get_intersection_node_set(headA, headB):
    seen = set()
    p = headA
    while p:
        seen.add(p)
        p = p.next
    p = headB
    while p:
        if p in seen:
            return p
        p = p.next
    return None

cons: Must redirect only after reaching null, so both pointers become null simultaneously if no intersection
approaches.timeExplanation: Each pointer takes at most len(A) + len(B) steps.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Uses only two pointer variables.

Trapping Rain Water.statement: Given nonnegative column heights of unit width, return the total water trapped between them after rain.
Trapping Rain Water.idea: Maintain leftMax and rightMax with two pointers at opposite ends. Whichever side has the lower boundary determines the water level at that pointer, because unseen interior walls can only be taller!
steps: left = 0, right = n - 1, leftMax = 0, rightMax = 0, water = 0.
Trapping Rain Water.python:
# Approach 2: Two pointers (Optimal)
def trap(height):
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = water = 0

    while left <= right:
        if left_max <= right_max:
            left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
            water += left_max - height[left]
            left += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[right])
            water += right_max - height[right]
            right -= 1

    return water

# Approach 1: Prefix & suffix max arrays
def trap(height):
    n = len(height)
    if n <= 2:
        return 0
    left_max = [0] * n
    right_max = [0] * n
    left_max[0] = height[0]
    for i in range(1, n):
        left_max[i] = max(left_max[i - 1], height[i])
    right_max[n - 1] = height[n - 1]
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        right_max[i] = max(right_max[i + 1], height[i])

    water = sum(min(left_max[i], right_max[i]) - height[i] for i in range(n))
    return water

# Approach 1: Sliding window with set
def length_of_longest_substring(s: str) -> int:
    seen = set()
    left = max_len = 0
    for right, c in enumerate(s):
        while c in seen:
            seen.remove(s[left])
            left += 1
        seen.add(c)
        max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)
    return max_len

Longest Repeating Character Replacement.idea: Maintain a sliding window [left, right] and track the maximum frequency of any character in the current window (maxFreq). If (windowLength - maxFreq) > k, we have more than k characters to replace, so shrink the window by advancing left.

# Approach 1: Sliding Window (Optimal)
# Slide window ensuring (window_len - max_freq) <= k
def character_replacement(s: str, k: int) -> int:
    count = {}
    left = 0
    max_freq = 0
    max_len = 0

    for right in range(len(s)):
        count[s[right]] = count.get(s[right], 0) + 1
        max_freq = max(max_freq, count[s[right]])

        if (right - left + 1) - max_freq > k:
            count[s[left]] -= 1
            left += 1

        max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)

    return max_len

Sliding Window Maximum.statement: For every contiguous window of k elements in an array, return its maximum; 1 ≤ k ≤ array length.
Sliding Window Maximum.idea: Use a double-ended queue (deque) storing indices. Maintain elements in strictly decreasing order of value: when inserting nums[i], pop from back while elements are smaller. Also drop indices older than i - k + 1 from front. The front of the deque is always the maximum of the current window!
steps: For each index i from 0 to N - 1:
Remove indices out of window bounds: if front <= i - k, pop_front.
Maintain decreasing order: while back element <= nums[i], pop_back.
Push i to back of deque.
If i >= k - 1, append nums[deque.front()] to result.
Sliding Window Maximum.python:
# Approach 1: Monotonic Deque (Optimal)
# Double-ended queue tracks window maximum
from collections import deque

def max_sliding_window(nums, k):
    dq = deque()  # Stores indices
    result = []

    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        # Remove elements out of window
        if dq and dq[0] <= i - k:
            dq.popleft()

        # Remove elements smaller than current from back
        while dq and nums[dq[-1]] <= x:
            dq.pop()

        dq.append(i)

        # Record max once window is fully formed
        if i >= k - 1:
            result.append(nums[dq[0]])

    return result

# Approach 1: Recursive Preorder
def preorder_traversal(root):
    res = []
    def dfs(node):
        if not node:
            return
        res.append(node.val)
        dfs(node.left)
        dfs(node.right)
    dfs(root)
    return res

            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()
        res.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.right

# Approach 2: Recursive DFS with Depth Tracking

def level_order_dfs(root):

            return
        if depth == len(result):
            result.append([])
        result[depth].append(node.val)
        dfs(node.left, depth + 1)
        dfs(node.right, depth + 1)

# Approach 2: Iterative Queue Comparison
# Enqueue mirror pairs
from collections import deque

def is_symmetric_iterative(root):
    if not root:
        return True
    q = deque([root.left, root.right])

    while q:
        t1 = q.popleft()
        t2 = q.popleft()

        if not t1 and not t2:
            continue
        if not t1 or not t2 or t1.val != t2.val:
            return False

        q.append(t1.left)
        q.append(t2.right)
        q.append(t1.right)
        q.append(t2.left)

    return True

# Approach 1: Recursive DFS (Optimal)
# Invert subtrees and swap left/right
def invert_tree(root):
    if not root:
        return None

    root.left, root.right = invert_tree(root.right), invert_tree(root.left)
    return root

Same Tree.statement: Determine whether two trees have equal structure and equal values.
Same Tree.idea: Two trees p and q are the same if: both are null (true), one is null (false), p.val == q.val, and recursively isSameTree(p.left, q.left) && isSameTree(p.right, q.right).
steps: If both p and q are null, return true.
If one is null or p.val != q.val, return false.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Recursive Lockstep DFS (Optimal)
approaches.idea: Two trees p and q are the same if: both are null (true), one is null (false), p.val == q.val, and recursively isSameTree(p.left, q.left) && isSameTree(p.right, q.right).
pros: Short-circuits upon first value or structural mismatch

If one is null or p.val != q.val, return false.

approaches.name: Approach 2: Iterative Queue Lockstep (Alternative)

pros: No recursion call stack overflow risk
cons: Allocates memory for pair queue
steps: While queue not empty: pop (n1, n2). If both null continue; if one null or values differ return false.
approaches.timeExplanation: Processes corresponding pairs until mismatch or end.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Queue holds nodes at widest level.
approaches.python:
# Approach 2: Iterative Queue Comparison
# Queue-based lockstep pair comparison
from collections import deque

def is_same_tree_iterative(p, q):
    queue = deque([(p, q)])

    while queue:
        n1, n2 = queue.popleft()
        if not n1 and not n2:
            continue
        if not n1 or not n2 or n1.val != n2.val:
            return False

        queue.append((n1.left, n2.left))
        queue.append((n1.right, n2.right))

    return True

Balanced Binary Tree.idea: Compute height bottom-up. If any subtree is unbalanced, immediately return -1 as a sentinel signal to bubble up the failure, avoiding redundant height calculations.

Diameter of a Binary Tree.statement: Return the largest number of edges on any path between two nodes.
Diameter of a Binary Tree.idea: The diameter through any node is (leftHeight + rightHeight). In a single post-order traversal, each node computes its subtree height (1 + max(lh, rh)) while updating a global max diameter with (lh + rh).
steps: Helper height(node): if null return 0; lh = height(node.left); rh = height(node.right); diameter = max(diameter, lh + rh); return 1 + max(lh, rh).
Diameter of a Binary Tree.python:
# Approach 1: Bottom-Up Post-Order (Optimal)
# Update diameter while returning subtree heights
def diameter_of_binary_tree(root):
    max_diameter = 0

    def height(node):
        nonlocal max_diameter
        if not node:
            return 0
        lh = height(node.left)
        rh = height(node.right)
        max_diameter = max(max_diameter, lh + rh)
        return 1 + max(lh, rh)

    height(root)
    return max_diameter

Zigzag Level Order Traversal.statement: Group values by level, alternating left-to-right and right-to-left.
Zigzag Level Order Traversal.idea: Perform BFS level order traversal. Maintain a boolean flag 'leftToRight'. For each level, allocate an array of size levelSize: if leftToRight fill from index 0 upwards; else fill from index levelSize - 1 downwards. Flip flag after each level.
steps: If root is null, return empty list.
Initialize queue with root, leftToRight = true.
While queue not empty: size = q.size(); allocate level array of length size; fill from left or right based on flag; flip flag.
Zigzag Level Order Traversal.python:
# Approach 1: BFS with Direction Flag (Optimal)
# Fill list from start or end based on parity
from collections import deque

def zigzag_level_order(root):
    if not root:
        return []
    result = []
    q = deque([root])
    left_to_right = True

    while q:
        sz = len(q)
        row = [0] * sz
        for i in range(sz):
            node = q.popleft()
            idx = i if left_to_right else sz - 1 - i
            row[idx] = node.val
            if node.left: q.append(node.left)
            if node.right: q.append(node.right)

        left_to_right = not left_to_right
        result.append(row)

    return result

Lowest Common Ancestor.statement: Return the lowest node whose subtree contains both target node identities. Both targets exist.

Lowest Common Ancestor.idea: Recursively search for p and q. If current node is null or equals p or q, return current node. Search left and right subtrees: if both return non-null, current node is the LCA split point! If only one returns non-null, pass it up.
steps: If root is null or root == p or root == q, return root.
If left and right are both non-null, root is LCA.

Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum.statement: Find the largest sum along any nonempty simple path in a binary tree.
Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum.idea: At each node, compute the maximum contribution (gain) from the left and right subtrees (ignoring negative contributions using max(0, gain)). The maximum path passing THROUGH this node as an apex is node.val + leftGain + rightGain. Update the global max path sum, and return node.val + max(leftGain, rightGain) to parent.
steps: Helper maxGain(node): if null return 0; leftGain = max(0, maxGain(node.left)); rightGain = max(0, maxGain(node.right)).
Update maxSum = max(maxSum, node.val + leftGain + rightGain).
Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum.python:
# Approach 1: Post-Order Max Gain Helper (Optimal)
# Calculate one-way branch gain while updating global two-way apex sum
def max_path_sum(root):
    max_sum = float('-inf')

    def max_gain(node):
        nonlocal max_sum
        if not node:
            return 0
        left_gain = max(0, max_gain(node.left))
        right_gain = max(0, max_gain(node.right))

        max_sum = max(max_sum, node.val + left_gain + right_gain)
        return node.val + max(left_gain, right_gain)

    max_gain(root)
    return max_sum

# Approach 2: Early-Stopping In-Order (Optimal)
# Stop immediately at kth node
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    stack = []
    curr = root

    while curr or stack:
        while curr:
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return curr.val
        curr = curr.right

    return -1

Last Stone Weight.statement: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones; keep their difference if unequal. Return the remaining weight.
Last Stone Weight.idea: Insert all stone weights into a max-heap. In each step, pop the two heaviest stones y and x (with y >= x). If y != x, push (y - x) back into the heap. Repeat until at most 1 stone remains.

# Approach 1: Max-Heap Simulation (Optimal)
# Use inverted numbers for max-heap in Python
import heapq

def last_stone_weight(stones):
    heap = [-s for s in stones]
    heapq.heapify(heap)

    while len(heap) > 1:
        y = -heapq.heappop(heap)
        x = -heapq.heappop(heap)
        if y != x:
            heapq.heappush(heap, -(y - x))

    return -heap[0] if heap else 0

def combine(n: int, k: int):

    def backtrack(start, combo):

            res.append(list(combo))
            return
        needed = k - len(combo)

            backtrack(i + 1, combo)
            combo.pop()

    return res

def subsets_with_dup_set(nums):
    nums.sort()

            if candidates[i] > remain:

    return res

        if remain == 0:
            res.append(list(combo))
            return
        for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
            if candidates[i] > remain:
                break
            combo.append(candidates[i])
            backtrack(i, remain - candidates[i], combo)
            combo.pop()

    backtrack(0, target, [])
    return res

# Approach 1: Sort + Used Array (Optimal)
# Skip duplicates when predecessor is unused
def permute_unique(nums):
    nums.sort()
    res = []
    used = [False] * len(nums)
    path = []

    def backtrack():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            res.append(list(path))
            return
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1] and not used[i - 1]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(nums[i])
            backtrack()
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False

    backtrack()
    return res

# Approach 2: Frequency Map Backtracking
from collections import Counter

def permute_unique_freq(nums):
    counts = Counter(nums)
    res = []
    path = []

    def backtrack():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            res.append(list(path))
            return
        for num in counts:
            if counts[num] > 0:
                counts[num] -= 1
                path.append(num)
                backtrack()
                path.pop()
                counts[num] += 1

    backtrack()
    return res

N Queens.statement: Place n queens on an n by n board so no two share a row, column, or diagonal. Return every board.
N Queens.idea: Place one queen per row. A queen at (row, col) attacks column 'col', positive diagonal (row + col), and negative diagonal (row - col). Maintain three boolean sets/arrays to check safety in O(1) time!

If row == n, format board and append to result.

Place queen, insert into 3 sets, recurse row + 1, remove from sets and unplace.

# Approach 1: Backtracking with Diagonal Sets (Optimal)
# O(1) set lookup for columns and both diagonals
def solve_n_queens(n: int):
    res = []
    cols = set()
    pos_diag = set()  # r + c
    neg_diag = set()  # r - c
    board = [["."] * n for _ in range(n)]

    def backtrack(r):
        if r == n:
            res.append(["".join(row) for row in board])
            return
        for c in range(n):
            if c in cols or (r + c) in pos_diag or (r - c) in neg_diag:
                continue

            cols.add(c)
            pos_diag.add(r + c)
            neg_diag.add(r - c)
            board[r][c] = "Q"

            backtrack(r + 1)

            cols.remove(c)
            pos_diag.remove(r + c)
            neg_diag.remove(r - c)
            board[r][c] = "."

    backtrack(0)
    return res

Two City Scheduling.statement: Send exactly half of 2n people to each city while minimizing total travel cost.
Two City Scheduling.idea: Suppose we initially send all 2N people to city A (total cost = sum(costA)). If we redirect person i to city B instead of city A, the change in cost is (costB - costA). To minimize total cost, greedily pick the N people with the SMALLEST (costB - costA) and send them to city B!

Remaining N people fly to city B.

# Approach 1: Greedy Sorting by Cost Difference (Optimal)
# Sort by savings: (costA - costB)
def two_city_sched_cost(costs: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    costs.sort(key=lambda x: x[0] - x[1])

    n = len(costs) // 2
    cost_a = sum(costs[i][0] for i in range(n))
    cost_b = sum(costs[i][1] for i in range(n, 2 * n))

    return cost_a + cost_b

# Approach 2: State Machine DP
def max_profit_dp(prices):
    hold, cash = -prices[0], 0
    for p in prices[1:]:
        hold = max(hold, cash - p)
        cash = max(cash, hold + p)
    return cash

Phase 3: While i < N: append intervals[i], i++.

Task Scheduler.statement: Find the least CPU intervals needed when equal task labels must be separated by n idle or other-task intervals.
Task Scheduler.idea: Find the maximum frequency of any task (maxFreq) and how many tasks share this maximum frequency (maxCount). The most frequent tasks form (maxFreq - 1) frames of size (n + 1), followed by the final maxCount tasks. Minimum slots needed is max(tasks.length, (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + maxCount).
steps: Count frequencies of each task ('A' to 'Z').
Find maxFreq and maxCount (number of tasks with frequency == maxFreq).
Task Scheduler.python:
# Approach 1: Math Formula on Max Frequency (Optimal)
# Frame formula based on most frequent tasks
from collections import Counter

def least_interval(tasks: list[str], n: int) -> int:
    counts = Counter(tasks)
    max_freq = max(counts.values())
    max_count = sum(1 for f in counts.values() if f == max_freq)

    empty_slots = (max_freq - 1) * (n + 1) + max_count
    return max(len(tasks), empty_slots)

Gas Station.statement: Find a starting station from which a car with an initially empty tank can complete the circular route, or -1.
Gas Station.idea: If total gas < total cost, completing the circuit is impossible (-1). Otherwise, a valid starting station is GUARANTEED to exist! Maintain a running tank: whenever running tank drops below 0, no station from our start up to current station can be valid, so reset tank to 0 and set starting station = current + 1.
Gas Station.python:
# Approach 1: Single-Pass Greedy Reset (Optimal)
# Track total surplus and reset start when current tank dips negative
def can_complete_circuit(gas: list[int], cost: list[int]) -> int:
    total_surplus = 0
    current_tank = 0
    start_station = 0

    for i in range(len(gas)):
        diff = gas[i] - cost[i]
        total_surplus += diff
        current_tank += diff

        if current_tank < 0:
            start_station = i + 1
            current_tank = 0

    return start_station if total_surplus >= 0 else -1

# Approach 2: DP Array (Standard)
def min_cost_climbing_stairs_dp(cost: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(cost)

    return dp[n]

# Approach 2: Tabular DP Array
def rob_dp(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    if n == 0: return 0
    if n == 1: return nums[0]

    dp = [0] * n
    dp[0] = nums[0]
    dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1])

    for i in range(2, n):
        dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + nums[i])
    return dp[n - 1]

Palindromic Substrings.idea: A palindrome mirrors around its center. In a string of length N, there are 2N - 1 possible centers: N single-character centers (odd length) and N - 1 pair centers (even length). For each center, expand outward while characters match, incrementing the count.

# Approach 1: Expand Around Centers (Optimal)
# Expand from 2N - 1 centers with O(1) extra space
def count_substrings(s: str) -> int:
    total = 0

    def count_around(l, r):
        cnt = 0
        while l >= 0 and r < len(s) and s[l] == s[r]:
            cnt += 1
            l -= 1
            r += 1
        return cnt

    for i in range(len(s)):
        total += count_around(i, i)      # Odd length
        total += count_around(i, i + 1)  # Even length

    return total

# Approach 2: Tabular DP Array
def num_decodings_dp(s: str) -> int:
    if not s or s[0] == '0': return 0
    n = len(s)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    dp[0] = 1
    dp[1] = 1

    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        if s[i - 1] != '0': dp[i] += dp[i - 1]
        val = int(s[i - 2 : i])
        if 10 <= val <= 26: dp[i] += dp[i - 2]

    return dp[n]

Maximum Product Subarray.statement: Return the largest product of any nonempty contiguous subarray.
Maximum Product Subarray.idea: Because multiplying two negative numbers creates a positive product, a very negative product can instantly flip into a large positive maximum! At each index, maintain both maxProd and minProd. When encountering a negative number, swap maxProd and minProd before updating.
steps: Initialize maxProd = nums[0], minProd = nums[0], result = nums[0].
If num < 0, swap maxProd and minProd.
Maximum Product Subarray.python:
# Approach 1: Kadane's Variant (Optimal)
# Track min and max products, swapping on negatives
def max_product(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    max_prod = nums[0]
    min_prod = nums[0]
    result = nums[0]

    for x in nums[1:]:
        if x < 0:
            max_prod, min_prod = min_prod, max_prod

        max_prod = max(x, max_prod * x)
        min_prod = min(x, min_prod * x)

        result = max(result, max_prod)

    return result

# Approach 2: Prefix and Suffix Scan
def max_product_scan(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    left, right, res = 0, 0, nums[0]
    for i in range(n):
        left = (left or 1) * nums[i]
        right = (right or 1) * nums[n - 1 - i]
        res = max(res, left, right)
    return res

Jump Game II.idea: Think of jumps as BFS levels: level 0 is [0, 0]. In each jump, we can reach anywhere up to the farthest reachable index from the current level. Maintain 'currEnd' (boundary of current jump) and 'farthest'. When i reaches currEnd, we must take another jump (jumps++) and extend currEnd = farthest.

# Approach 1: Greedy BFS Interval Levels (Optimal)
# Increment jumps when reaching current jump boundary
def jump(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    if n <= 1:
        return 0

    jumps = 0
    curr_end = 0
    farthest = 0

    for i in range(n - 1):
        farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])

        if i == curr_end:
            jumps += 1
            curr_end = farthest
            if curr_end >= n - 1:
                break

    return jumps

Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick.idea: Add stick ends [0, n] to cuts and sort: A = [0, cuts..., n]. Now any cut at index k costs (A[j] - A[i]) and splits the problem into independent subproblems [i, k] and [k, j]. dp[i][j] = (A[j] - A[i]) + min_{i < k < j}(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]).

Initialize 2D memo table of size M x M with 0.
dp(i, j): if j - i <= 1 return 0 (no cuts inside); try all cut positions k between i and j; cost = (A[j] - A[i]) + min(dp(i, k) + dp(k, j)).

# Approach 1: Hierholzer's Eulerian Path Algorithm (Optimal)
# Hierholzer's algorithm on directed multigraph
from collections import defaultdict

def find_itinerary(tickets: list[list[str]]) -> list[str]:
    adj = defaultdict(list)
    # Sort reverse so pop() takes the smallest lexicographical airport in O(1)
    for u, v in sorted(tickets, reverse=True):
        adj[u].append(v)

    route = []

    def dfs(airport):
        while adj[airport]:
            dfs(adj[airport].pop())
        route.append(airport)

    dfs("JFK")
    return route[::-1]

# Approach 2: Disjoint Set Union
def make_connected_dsu(n, connections):
    if len(connections) < n - 1: return -1
    p = list(range(n))
    def find(i):
        if p[i] == i: return i
        p[i] = find(p[i])
        return p[i]

    comps = n
    for u, v in connections:
        r1, r2 = find(u), find(v)
        if r1 != r2:
            p[r1] = r2
            comps -= 1
    return comps - 1

# Approach 1: Dijkstra with Path Count Accumulation (Optimal)
# Dijkstra tracking shortest distances and counts simultaneously
import heapq

def count_paths(n: int, roads: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    MOD = 10**9 + 7
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, time in roads:
        adj[u].append((v, time))
        adj[v].append((u, time))

    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    ways = [0] * n
    dist[0] = 0
    ways[0] = 1

    pq = [(0, 0)]  # (distance, node)

    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue

        for v, time in adj[u]:
            new_dist = d + time
            if new_dist < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = new_dist
                ways[v] = ways[u]
                heapq.heappush(pq, (new_dist, v))
            elif new_dist == dist[v]:
                ways[v] = (ways[v] + ways[u]) % MOD

    return ways[n - 1]

# Approach 1: Prim's Algorithm (Optimal for Complete Graphs)
# Dense-graph Prim's algorithm in O(N^2) time and O(N) space
def min_cost_connect_points(points: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    n = len(points)
    min_dist = [float('inf')] * n
    in_mst = [False] * n
    min_dist[0] = 0
    total_cost = 0

    for _ in range(n):
        # Pick unvisited node with minimum distance to tree
        u = -1
        for i in range(n):
            if not in_mst[i] and (u == -1 or min_dist[i] < min_dist[u]):
                u = i

        in_mst[u] = True
        total_cost += min_dist[u]

        # Update neighbors
        x1, y1 = points[u]
        for v in range(n):
            if not in_mst[v]:
                dist = abs(x1 - points[v][0]) + abs(y1 - points[v][1])
                if dist < min_dist[v]:
                    min_dist[v] = dist

    return total_cost

def min_cost_connect_points(points: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    n = len(points)
    min_dist = [float('inf')] * n
    in_mst = [False] * n
    min_dist[0] = 0
    total_cost = 0

    for _ in range(n):
        # Pick unvisited node with minimum distance to tree
        u = -1
        for i in range(n):
            if not in_mst[i] and (u == -1 or min_dist[i] < min_dist[u]):
                u = i

        in_mst[u] = True
        total_cost += min_dist[u]

        # Update neighbors
        x1, y1 = points[u]
        for v in range(n):
            if not in_mst[v]:
                dist = abs(x1 - points[v][0]) + abs(y1 - points[v][1])
                if dist < min_dist[v]:
                    min_dist[v] = dist

    return total_cost

approaches.name: Approach 2: Kruskal's Algorithm with DSU (Alternative)
approaches.idea: Generate all N*(N-1)/2 edges with their Manhattan distances. Sort all edges ascending by weight. Use Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) to greedily add edges that connect different components until N - 1 edges are added.
cons: O(N² log N) runtime and O(N²) memory to store and sort all edges
steps: Generate all pair edges [dist, u, v].
DSU: union endpoints, accumulate cost until n - 1 edges selected.
approaches.timeExplanation: Sorts N² edges.
approaches.spaceExplanation: Stores all N*(N - 1)/2 edges.
